titleText.es: Está celoso porque todo el mundo está en el desván escuchando a Stephen Colbert.
titleText.en: He's jealous because everyone is up in the attic listening to Stephen Colbert.
titleText.noteEn: The official English title text adds “just” before “jealous”; the Spanish archive keeps the same attic-and-Colbert joke without that extra emphasis.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: strike; organized work stoppage
cardDefinitions.noteEn: A huelga is a collective refusal to work, usually used to press for changes in pay or working conditions.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: screenwriters; scriptwriters
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Guionista names someone who writes scripts for film, television, radio, or similar productions. The same ending is used for men and women; the article shows the gender when needed.

example.es: Las guionistas preparan una nueva serie.
example.en: The screenwriters are preparing a new series.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: awful; terrible (in ser una mierda, vulgar)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Mierda literally means “shit.” In the vulgar judgment ser una mierda, it describes something as very bad, worthless, or deeply unpleasant rather than naming a literal substance.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: you watch (informal singular, television or a show)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Ver normally means “to see,” but with television, films, or shows it often corresponds to English “watch.” Ves is the present form for one person addressed informally.

example.en: Do you watch that series on Mondays?

cardDefinitions.answerEn: TV series; shows
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Serie has the same spelling pattern as English “series,” but Spanish uses series as the plural form.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: true; right (showing agreement)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Used as a brief response, cierto confirms that the preceding point is correct. This differs from cierto before a noun, where it can mean “a certain.”

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I ended up
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Acabé is a completed-past form for the speaker. Before an action ending in -ando or -iendo, acabar can describe the final, sometimes unintended result: acabé riendo means “I ended up laughing.”

example.en: I ended up accepting the proposal.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: getting fed up; becoming tired of it (the speaker)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hartarse means to become fed up. The -ando form presents that change as an ongoing action, and the attached me identifies the speaker.

example.en: I'm getting fed up with the noise.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: couple; pair
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Un par de before a plural noun commonly means “a couple of,” often an approximate small quantity rather than an exact matched pair.

example.en: I need a couple of minutes.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: weeks
you stopped (informal singular, completed past)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In dejar de followed by an unchanged action verb, dejaste says that one person addressed informally stopped doing that activity.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to follow; keep track of (events or news)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Seguir can mean to follow developing news, a campaign, a competition, or another continuing sequence of events—not only to move behind someone physically.

example.en: I follow the news every day.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: election campaign
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Campaña can name an organized effort. With electoral or in a political setting, it means an election campaign.

example.en: The election campaign starts in April.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: on; engaged in (as part of estar en campaña)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish uses en between estar and campaña to describe being actively engaged in a campaign. Natural English often says “campaigning” or “on the campaign trail.”

cardDefinitions.answerEn: electoral; related to an election
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Electoral has one form for masculine and feminine singular nouns: proceso electoral and campaña electoral.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: commentary; comments
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Comentarios can mean individual comments or ongoing spoken analysis and commentary about events.

example.es: Escuchamos sus comentarios sobre el partido.
example.en: We listened to her commentary on the match.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: by; from (identifying the creator or source)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: De can connect a work, statement, or piece of commentary to the person who created or supplied it. Natural English often uses “by” rather than literal “of.”

example.en: I read an article by Marta.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I kidnapped; I abducted
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Secuestré is the completed-past form for the speaker. Its written accent keeps the stress on the final syllable.

example.es: En la película, el villano secuestró al científico.
example.en: In the film, the villain kidnapped the scientist.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: he would do; he did (special past form after para que)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hiciera is a special past form of hacer used when a past action states the purpose or desired result of another past action. Ordinary hizo changes to hiciera after a frame such as para que.

example.es: Le escribí para que hiciera una copia.
example.en: I wrote to him so that he would make a copy.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: analyses; pieces of analysis
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Análisis keeps the same written form in singular and plural. A plural article or another plural word shows when more than one analysis is meant.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: locked up; shut in (masculine singular)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Encerrado describes the resulting state of a masculine singular person or thing after being confined or shut inside.

example.es: El perro está encerrado en el patio.
example.en: The dog is shut in the yard.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: basement
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The written accent belongs on the first syllable: sótano.

example.es: Guardamos las cajas en el sótano.
example.en: We keep the boxes in the basement.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: is; currently ranks (in ir primero, “to be leading”)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In a ranking, a form of ir followed by primero, segunda, and so on gives the current position. Va primero means that one person or team is in first place.

example.en: Our team is in first place.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: first; in first place (masculine singular)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: After a movement verb such as ir, primero can state a current rank rather than the order in which actions happen.

example.es: Daniel va primero en la carrera.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: make me; give me (informal singular command)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Haz is the irregular positive command of hacer for one person addressed informally. Me attaches to its end and identifies the speaker as the person receiving or benefiting from what is made.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: comment; piece of commentary
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Comentario can be a written or spoken comment, including a short observation about current events.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: sharp; perceptive; witty (masculine singular)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: For a remark or analysis, agudo describes quick, penetrating intelligence. In other settings it can instead describe a high-pitched sound or a sharp point.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: and (used instead of y before an i sound)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Spanish changes y to e before a following word that begins with the vowel sound i, which makes the two words easier to distinguish in speech.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: let; allow (informal singular command)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Deja is the positive command for one person addressed informally. Before que and another action, it asks that person to allow the action.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; links dejar to the allowed action
cardDefinitions.noteEn: After a form of dejar meaning “let” or “allow,” que introduces the allowed action. The person doing that action may be stated after que or understood from the situation and the verb form.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: me (the speaker as the person allowed to act)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: In a request such as deja que me siente, me belongs with the following action and identifies the speaker. Natural English likewise uses “me” after “let.”

cardDefinitions.answerEn: I leave; I go (special form after deja que)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: After deja que, the ordinary first-person form voy changes to vaya because the action is being requested or allowed rather than stated as a fact.

example.es: Mi madre deja que vaya solo.
example.en: My mother lets me go alone.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: ser una mierda, para juzgar algo
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can vulgar informal Spanish say that something is awful or worthless?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of ser followed by una mierda.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This fixed vulgar judgment literally uses the noun mierda, “shit,” but the whole expression describes a person, thing, or situation as very bad. Change ser for the person and time; una mierda stays fixed.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that a candidate or political team is actively campaigning?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by en campaña, optionally adding electoral.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time, while en campaña names the active campaign period. Electoral makes the election meaning explicit; without it, the surrounding political context can do that work.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: acabar seguido de una acción en -ando o -iendo
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone eventually ends up doing something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of acabar followed directly by the action in its -ando or -iendo form.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Only acabar changes for the person and time. The second action uses the ongoing form ending in -ando or -iendo, often called a gerund. This pattern gives the eventual result, which may be unintended: acabamos riendo means “we ended up laughing.”

example.en: We ended up talking all afternoon.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say “a couple of” before a plural noun?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use un par de, then the plural noun.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The literal idea is a pair, but conversational un par de often gives an approximate small quantity. The noun after de is plural: un par de días, un par de preguntas.

example.en: I have a couple of questions.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone or a team is currently in first place?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of ir followed by primero or primera to match the person or team being ranked.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Ir changes for the person and time. Primero changes to primera for a feminine singular person or thing, and plural rankings use primeros or primeras. The expression states a current position, not physical movement.

example.en: Our team is in first place.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: e en lugar de y antes de un sonido i
cardDefinitions.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes use e where you expect y for “and”?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Change y to e before a word that begins with the vowel sound i.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The change avoids placing two similar i sounds together: padres e hijos. It is based on sound, not merely spelling, so y normally remains before words beginning with the consonant-like sound in hie-, as in nieve y hielo.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: dejar que otra persona haga algo
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone lets or allows another person to do something?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, then que, then put the allowed action in its special requested-action form; state the person when the context does not already make them clear.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive because the action is being allowed or requested, not stated as an established fact. For example, ordinary decide changes to decida, and ordinary busco changes to busque. The person can be explicit, as in deja que Ana decida, or understood from the action form and situation, as in deja que busque, “let me search.” Dejar changes for the person and time; que remains unchanged.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can Spanish state the general fact of having a possession or family relationship without using un or una?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of tener followed directly by the singular noun when the general fact of having it is what matters.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Common examples include tener coche, tener casa, and tener familia. Natural English usually supplies ‘a’ in ‘have a car/house/family.’ Spanish often adds un or una when counting, emphasizing one particular item, or describing it: tengo una casa pequeña.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: huelga de guionistas · Jon Stewart y los comentarios políticos
cardDefinitions.answerEn: The joke refers to the 2007–08 U.S. writers' strike interrupting scripted television, including topical political comedy.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Jon Stewart hosted The Daily Show, whose writers helped produce its satirical analysis of current campaigns. The comic makes Black Hat solve the missing-commentary problem by kidnapping Stewart; the title text moves rival host Stephen Colbert to the attic.

regions.labelEs: ESTA HUELGA DE GUIONISTAS ES UNA MIERDA. TÚ NO VES SERIES.

applications.explanationEn: Es supplies the present form of ser, while una mierda forms the fixed vulgar negative judgment.
Tú is stated for contrast even though ves already identifies informal singular “you”; no supplies the negation between them.
Por and accented qué are written as two words because they directly ask for a reason.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, PERO ES UNA MIERDA ESTAR EN CAMPAÑA ELECTORAL SIN LOS COMENTARIOS DE JON STEWART.

excludedUnits.rationale: Jon is an English given name, not a Spanish lexical word.
Stewart is a surname, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Es supplies the present form of ser, while una mierda forms the fixed vulgar negative judgment.
Estar stays in its dictionary form after the preceding judgment, while en campaña electoral names the active election-campaign state.

regions.labelEs: CIERTO. ACABÉ HARTÁNDOME HACE UN PAR DE SEMANAS.

applications.explanationEn: Acabé gives the completed past viewpoint, and hartándome supplies the -ando action that became the eventual result for the speaker.
Hace comes before the complete duration un par de semanas to place the earlier change that far back from the present.
Un par de supplies the small approximate quantity, and semanas is the plural time noun being counted.
Dejaste gives the completed past form for informal singular “you,” de is required by the pattern, and seguir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: NO. SECUESTRÉ A JON STEWART PARA QUE ME HICIERA SUS ANÁLISIS.

excludedUnits.rationale: Jon is an English given name, not a Spanish lexical word.
Stewart is a surname, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: A appears before the specific person directly affected by secuestré; the two name tokens remain excluded from the Spanish vocabulary cards.

applications.exampleEs: PARA QUE ME HICIERA SUS ANÁLISIS
applications.explanationEn: Para que introduces the intended result, me identifies its beneficiary, and hiciera is the special past form because the analysis was the purpose of another past action.

words.geometryRationale: The Vision box extends well below the one-word reaction into the nearby character; this measured box follows only the printed question.

applications.explanationEn: Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks for information, even as a one-word question.
Está gives the present state, and masculine singular encerrado describes the result of someone having been confined.

regions.labelEs: ¡JON, OBAMA VA PRIMERO EN IOWA! ¡HAZME UN COMENTARIO AGUDO E IRÓNICO SOBRE LA SITUACIÓN!

excludedUnits.rationale: Jon is an English given name, not a Spanish lexical word.
Obama is a surname, not a Spanish lexical word.
Iowa is an English place name retained unchanged, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Va matches the single person being ranked, and masculine singular primero states the current first-place position.
Haz is the irregular positive tú command of hacer; the attached me does not change which command form is used.
Me is attached to the end of the positive command haz and the result is written as the single word hazme.
The usual y becomes e because irónico begins with the vowel sound i.

regions.labelEs: POR FAVOR, DEJA QUE ME VAYA. TENGO FAMILIA.

applications.explanationEn: Por and favor work together as the fixed politeness expression rather than contributing their usual separate meanings.
Deja is the positive command for one person addressed informally.
Deja requests permission from the listener, que opens the allowed action, me identifies the speaker, and ordinary voy changes to the requested-action form vaya.
Tengo states the general fact of having family, so familia follows directly without un or una even though natural English normally supplies ‘a.’
